impact.location_description: Off the eastern coast of Luzon Island, Philippines, during Typhoon Yagi; airburst at ~25 km altitude
impact.context: Coastal/near-shore, daytime, storm conditions (Typhoon Yagi overhead); witnessed and filmed by residents in Luzon through gaps in typhoon cloud cover, an unusual detection circumstance.

orbit.source: JPL SBDB, fetched 2026-09-07 (repo data/sbdb_orbits.txt); nobs=76 used in JPL fit (excludes 92 observations from station D29) vs 187 in MPC total

sensor_detections: US government satellite sensors, 0.2 kt at 18.0N 122.9E
confirmation.eyewitness: Videos from residents on Luzon captured the fireball through breaks in Typhoon Yagi's cloud cover; widely shared on social media and picked up by regional press.

scientific_results: ESA's independent impact-energy model (0.19 kt) matched the US government sensor measurement (0.2 kt) closely, one of the better agreements in the whole 13-object series and a useful validation point for airburst energy modeling.

Demonstrated real-time public tracking: ESA and JPL published the predicted impact time and location publicly before the event, and it was confirmed to within about 0.1 seconds and 100 meters — illustrating how precise short-arc orbit determination inside Earth's gravity well has become for imminent impactors.

JPL's SBDB fit excludes 92 of the 187 MPC-logged observations (station D29), a data-quality flag noted in this dataset's own orbit-fitting notes rather than in published literature; it does not appear to affect the impact solution's reliability given independent sensor confirmation.
No meteorite recovery was attempted; any surviving fragments would have fallen into the sea off Luzon.
narrative: Catalina Sky Survey technologist Jacqueline Fazekas discovered 2024 RW1 with the Mount Lemmon telescope at 06:39 UTC on 4 September 2024; automated systems quickly computed a high-confidence impact solution pointing at the Philippines less than eleven hours later. The object entered Earth's atmosphere at 16:39 UTC that same day, close to the eastern coast of Luzon, while Typhoon Yagi was moving through the region — an unusual coincidence that both obscured the fireball from many potential witnesses and produced striking footage from those who caught it through breaks in the storm clouds. US government sensors registered a 0.2-kilotons detonation matching ESA's independently modeled 0.19 kt almost exactly, one of the closest measured-to-modeled agreements among the 13 known pre-impact detections. It was only the ninth asteroid ever spotted before hitting Earth, and its predicted time and location proved accurate to within roughly a tenth of a second and 100 meters.
